description: We’re five Research Master’s students in Business Analytics at Tunis Business School, with backgrounds in business intelligence, management, and economics. We bring Python, R, dashboarding, web development, and data engineering, all driven by a passion for data and AI. We’re organized, collaborative, and aim for results we’re proud of. We’re looking for teammates with machine learning, software engineering, or strong storytelling and presentation skills. Curious and reliable people welcome!
summary: Fire Watch is a web app that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for North Africa (Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia). NASA’s fire record comes from two instruments: MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012. VIIRS detects 4–5 times more hotspots, so simply joining the two creates a fake jump in fire activity. We harmonized them statistically. A negative binomial model first corrects the 2002 jump caused by Aqua joining Terra. A second model, chosen among GLMs and machine-learning challengers on unseen years (2020 onward), translates MODIS counts into VIIRS equivalents for 2000–2011, with honest prediction intervals. Users draw any area on a map and see its normal fire season, past critical periods, anomalies and how this year compares with normal, then download the data. This gives responders, land managers and scientists a reliable long-term fire history and early-warning signals, so they can plan for fire seasons instead of reacting to them.
details:
What it does

Fire Lens turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire data into one easy fire calendar for North Africa (Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia). Pick any area on a map and see, week by week since 2000:

when fires normally happen

which periods were unusually intense

whether this year is above or below normal

You can also download the data as a CSV.

The problem

NASA uses two satellite instruments: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). VIIRS sees much smaller fires and counts 4-5 times more of them. If you simply join the two records, fire activity appears to jump in 2012 when nothing really changed. A smaller jump appears in 2002, when MODIS added a second satellite. This makes long-term trends misleading.

How it works

Clean the data. Both instruments get the same rules: only reliable detections, only vegetation fires, no duplicates.

Count on a common grid. Fires are counted per month in equal-size map cells.

Fix 2002. A statistical model estimates what two satellites would have seen when only one was flying.

Match MODIS to VIIRS. We learn how the two relate in the years they overlap (2012 onward), then apply that to 2000-2011.

Pick the best model. We test many models on years they haven’t seen. The winner has the lowest error and honest uncertainty ranges.

Show uncertainty. Estimated years before 2012 are labelled and shown with ranges.

Analyse. The app shows a normal year, unusually intense weeks, critical periods (2+ intense weeks in a row), and an early-warning curve for the current year.

The web app

FireWatch is a wildfire monitoring dashboard built for the NASA hackathon. It lets users explore fire activity through an overview with key numbers and charts, an interactive map of where fires occur, a calendar view of seasonal and monthly patterns, and deeper analytics for comparing trends. It also explains how multiple data sources were harmonized into one dataset.

Benefits

Fair history: the sensor change no longer looks like a real change in fires.

Emergency teams: know the normal fire season and whether this year is running high.

Land managers and scientists: see past critical periods, trends, and the uncertainty.

Easy to use: bilingual, colour-blind-safe, no GIS skills needed.

Results so far

Harmonization removes the artificial 2012 jump. The raw VIIRS record shows about 6× more hotspots than MODIS. After harmonization, average yearly activity before and after 2012 is nearly the same (about 0.93×).

At country level, the selected model has 54% lower error than a simple ratio on validation years 2015-2017.

On the untouched 2020+ test, its 90% ranges cover 87% of real values at country level and 90% at the 100 km cell level.

Our goal

A free, open tool that civil-protection and forestry agencies and researchers in North Africa can use to plan fire seasons. It can later extend to other regions and newer satellites (NOAA-20, NOAA-21).

Tools

Analysis: Python (Google Colab), pandas, NumPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, LightGBM

Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), Natural Earth borders

Web app: Cursor / Supabase / Node.js / React.js/ python/ Github/ Render]

Hardware: standard laptops only
